rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the just divine verdict, no one can aid the unjust.
rows.anchor: The day God will deliver His verdict with justice none will be able to help the unjust.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idols and intercessors have no divine sanction or knowledge; associating them with God without permission fabricates a lie against Him and is the gravest injustice.
rows.anchor: The deities and intercessors they associate with God are baseless. Neither has God sanctioned them nor do they have any knowledge regarding this matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling something a deity without a rational or natural basis rests on conjecture, which cannot replace knowledge or truth.
rows.anchor: without any logical or natural argument to support this claim is like following conjecture and conjecture can never replace knowledge and the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yastūn means to attack someone.
rows.anchor:
means “to attack someone.”
The implication is that though

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their fury at clear monotheistic proofs exposes their bias: they writhe in anger and appear ready to assault the reciters.
rows.anchor: when they are presented with lucid arguments in its favour, they writhe in frenzy and their faces convulse in anger and it looks as if they will attack those who recite these revelations before them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to warn that Hell will cause even greater revulsion; the disbelievers must face it as their evil abode.
rows.anchor: they should be informed by the Prophet (sws) of a thing that will distort their faces even more and they shall necessarily face it: the fire of Hell and it is a very evil abode.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fly exemplifies false deities' helplessness: even collective effort cannot create one, and they cannot recover what it snatches.
rows.anchor: This verse depicts the baselessness of their deities with a powerful example.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People regard a deity as a remedy for their own weakness, yet these foolish worshippers seek help from beings even more helpless than themselves.
rows.anchor: if a person regards someone to be a deity, it is because this is a remedy to his own frailty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They fail to recognize God's majesty; unlike their helpless idols, He is powerful and dominant, able to realize His will without impediment.
rows.anchor: He is not someone helpless like their deities. On the contrary, He is very powerful and dominant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels are neither God's daughters nor partners but servants; some are selected as envoys and sent to His messengers.
rows.anchor: Angels are not His daughters or partners. They are in fact His servants. Their only status is that some special ones among them are selected as His envoys

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God hears and sees everything, He has no need to make anyone His partner.
rows.anchor: since God hears and sees all, what need does He have to make anyone His partner?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God watches the angels' obligations, so they cannot exceed their prescribed bounds.
rows.anchor: He is also watching over the obligations of the angels – they dare not exceed the prescribed bounds in the slightest way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything behind and before the angels is within God's knowledge; they cannot add to it, conceal their acts, or claim knowledge God lacks.
rows.anchor: Whatever is behind and after these angels is in God’s knowledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All matters are presented to God, never to angels; reports of tasks assigned to the angels are presented to God.
rows.anchor: All matters are presented before God. They are neither presented before the angels nor will they ever be.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding verses follow the proof that Quraysh disbelievers are traitors, unfit to guard the House or inherit Abraham's legacy.
rows.anchor: of the Quraysh were proven as traitors and deceivers and thereby unworthy of being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Muslims expelled from the House are its truly worthy custodians.
rows.anchor: the real worthy custodians of this House of God are the Muslims who had been expelled from there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims have authority to wage jihad to liberate the House from occupation and cleanse it; these verses guide them in fulfilling that responsibility.
rows.anchor: They had also been given the authority to wage jihād to liberate the House of God from their occupation and cleanse it from filth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commands address the Muslims' promised leadership, a position of both privilege and responsibility.
rows.anchor: This position is a great privilege and also a great responsibility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kneeling and prostrating signify prayer.
rows.anchor: kneeling and prostrating were mentioned the foremost. They actually signify the prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer language also stresses attentiveness and focus during prayer.
rows.anchor: when a prayer is mentioned in this way, the purpose is to also refer to attention and focus during the prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording also alludes especially to tahajjud, adherence to which is essential for bearing great responsibilities.
rows.anchor: Also specially alluded to is the tahajjud prayer adhering to which is essential to become worthy of great responsibilities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer diligence expresses gratitude and helps Muslims become worthy of their responsibility.
rows.anchor: expressing gratitude and becoming worthy of the responsibility were

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 41 sets out the duties of custodianship of the sanctuary and what God expects of those entrusted with leadership.
rows.anchor: Readers are advised to look up verse 41 of this sūrah in which Muslims are informed of the responsibilities of the custodianship of the Ḥaram

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship, which follows a more general command, includes obedience to God in every sphere of life.
rows.anchor: Worship also encompasses obedience. In other words, what is required is worshipping and showing obedience to Him in all spheres of life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to do good deeds is broad and here concerns especially recommended, rewarding, character-shaping deeds beyond obligatory acts.
rows.anchor: These deeds refer to ones which are not obligatory but are highly recommended and rewarding as a result.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Diligence in these deeds makes Muslims capable of the promised earthly authority and worthy of success in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: they will become capable enough to be given the position of authority in the land that they are being promised.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to strive for God's cause with life and resources continues the preparation in conduct demanded earlier.
rows.anchor: This is in tandem to the preparation they were earlier required to make regarding their conduct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here jihad is not warfare, which depends on conditions discussed earlier, but striving by every available means to make God's word supreme.
rows.anchor: striving for the cause of God through all possible means a person can muster for the purpose of making His word superior.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Striving in the most befitting way means avoiding half-hearted effort and being ready to sacrifice one's life.
rows.anchor: The words “in the most befitting way” refer to the fact that this striving should not be half-hearted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God chose the Muslims to deliver His final message to humankind.
rows.anchor: Who has chosen them for the responsibility of delivering His final message to mankind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After displacing Quraysh and Jews, God chose Muslims to lead other nations; they should fulfill this role with exemplary resolve.
rows.anchor: Hence they should rise to the occasion and do full justice to their

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the Jewish religion, this faith imposes no such constraints; God protected it, as a religion based on human nature, so Muslims can bear its heavy responsibility.
rows.anchor: there are no constraints in this religion for them the way they existed in the religion followed by the Jews.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's religion is the Muslims' ancestral legacy; the direct addressees are Ishmaelites, Abraham's descendants who took pride in that lineage.
rows.anchor: the real addressees are the Ishmaelites who were not only the progeny of Abraham (sws), they were also very proud of this lineage.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible syntactic analysis supplies an omitted verb meaning 'follow' before the phrase about Abraham's community.
rows.anchor: can be regarded to be suppressed before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers reading ijtabā as encompassing another contextually suitable verb, citing 5:2.
rows.anchor: can be regarded to encompass the meaning of another verb that suits the occasion.

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: Some scholars take the pronoun 'he' to refer to God.
rows.anchor: Some scholars regard the antecedent of the pronoun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes the pronoun to refer to Abraham's prayer in 2:129 that God make his descendants a Muslim nation.
rows.anchor: However, in my opinion, it refers to the prayer of Abraham (sws) mentioned in verse 129 of Sūrah al-Baqarah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the community Muslim recalls it as the fulfillment of Abraham's prayer and encourages Muslims to remember that history.
rows.anchor: The purpose of referring to this name in this supplication is to encourage Muslims by informing them that they are the manifestation of their father’s prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham did not coin Islam or Muslim: Islam is the natural state of all things and all prophets followed it; Abraham prayed for an Ishmaelite community called Muslim, and God gave it that name.
rows.anchor: Islam is the nature of all objects of this universe, as is indicated in verse 82 of S ūrah Āl ‘Imr ān. All prophets have always followed Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The witness wording echoes 2:142, where the community bears witness before people and the messenger before the community.
rows.anchor: has also been mentioned in verse 142 of Sūrah al-Baqarah thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community's testimony is to continue before mankind until Judgment; Islahi discusses the nature of this witness under 2:143.
rows.anchor: they should bear witness to it before mankind until the Day of Judement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending returns to prayer, zakāh, and holding to God, tying them to the community's witness; prayer and zakāh are the two pillars on which religious practice stands.
rows.anchor: On these two pillars stands the whole edifice of religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author treats holding fast to God and holding fast to God's rope as equivalent expressions.
rows.anchor: There is no difference in the expressions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To face hardships in this cause, Muslims should remain resolute, remember their Lord, hold fast to His Book, and trust His help, since He is the best guardian and helper.
rows.anchor: This is the remedy being suggested to the hardships that will be faced in this cause: they should adhere to their stance with full resolve and keep their Lord in remembrance and hold fast to His Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With this doxology the explanation of the sūrah is complete, and all gratitude is to God, Lord of the worlds.
rows.anchor: With these words, the explanation of this sū rah comes to its completion.
